questions.question: What does the Stefan-Boltzmann Law describe?
options: Total power radiated by a blackbody
questions.explanation: Stefan-Boltzmann Law: P = εσAT⁴, where P is total power radiated, ε is emissivity, σ is Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴), A is surface area, T is absolute temperature.

questions.question: Two objects at same temperature are placed in identical environments. Which radiates more heat?
questions.explanation: For objects at same temperature, radiative power depends on emissiivity ε and surface area A (P = εσAT⁴). Darker objects typically have higher emissivity (closer to 1). Larger area also increases radiation, but not specified which is larger.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of heat transfer in fluids?
questions.explanation: In fluids (liquids and gases), convection is the primary heat transfer mechanism due to fluid motion carrying thermal energy. Conduction occurs but is less efficient in fluids than in solids.

questions.question: A 0.5 kg aluminum block (c = 900 J/kg°C) heats from 20°C to 70°C. How much heat is added?
According to Wien's Law, if a star's temperature doubles, what happens to λ_max?
questions.explanation: Wien's displacement law: λ_max T = constant (b ≈ 2.9×10⁻³ m·K). So λ_max ∝ 1/T. If T doubles, λ_max halves. Hotter objects emit shorter wavelength radiation.

questions.question: What does thermal conductivity measure?
options: Ability to transfer heat by conduction
questions.explanation: Thermal conductivity (k) measures a material's ability to conduct heat. High k = good conductor (metals). Low k = good insulator (wood, foam). Units: W/(m·K).

questions.question: Why does a metal feel colder than wood at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: Metal has higher thermal conductivity than wood, so it conducts heat away from your hand faster, making it feel colder even at same temperature.

questions.question: The R-value of insulation measures:
questions.explanation: R-value = thickness/thermal conductivity = d/k. Higher R-value means better insulation (greater resistance to heat flow). Used in building insulation ratings.

phase-changes.title: Phase Changes Quiz
phase-changes.description: Test your understanding of phase transitions, latent heat, and the behavior of substances during phase changes
keyConcepts: Latent heat of fuision and vaporazation

formulas.description: Heat for melting/freeying (latent heat of fusion)
Heat for vaporazation/condazation (latent heat of vaporazation)
First Law of thermodynamics during phase change
Heat for temperature change plus phase change

questions.question: During a phase change at constant temperature, what happens to the heat added?
questions.explanation: During phase change at constant temperature, added heat (latent heat) goes into overcoming intermolecular forces, not increasing kinetic energy. Temperature remains constant until phase change completes.

questions.question: What is the latent heat of fusion for water?
questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion for water (melting/freezing) is 334 J/g or 3.34 × 10^5 J/kg. Latent heat of vaporization is 2260 J/g or 2.26 × 10^6 J/kg.

questions.question: Why does steam at 100°C cause more severe burns then water at 100°C?
options: Steam releases latent heat when condensing
questions.explanation: Steam at 100°C releases 2260 J/g of latent heat when it condenses on skin, in addition to the heat from cooling to body temperature. Water at 100°C only releases heat from cooling.

questions.question: On a phase diagram, what does the triple point represent?
options: Temerature above which has cannot liquefy
Point where all three phases coexist

questions.question: What happens to the boiling point of water at high altitude?
questions.explanation: Boiling point decreases with decreasing atmospheric pressure. At high altitude, pressure is lower, so water boils below 100°C.

questions.question: How much heat is needed to melt 50 g of ice at 0°C? (L_f = 334 J/g)
questions.explanation: Q = mL_f = 50 g × 334 J/g = 16,700 J = 16.7 kJ. No temperature change occurs during melting.

questions.question: What is sublimation?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is solid → gas without passing through liquid phase. Examples: dry ice (CO₂), iodine crystals, snow evaporating. Reverse process is deposition (gas → solid).

questions.question: During vaporization at constant temperature and pressure, what is true about internal energy change?
questions.explanation: From the 1st Law we know that ΔU = Q - W. During vaporazation at constant P, heat Q = mL_v is added, and work W = PΔV is done as liquid expands to gas. So ΔU = mL_v - PΔV.

questions.question: What does the critical point on a phase diagram represent?
options: Temperature above which liquid and gas are indistinguishable
Point where all phases have same density
questions.explanation: The critical point is the temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone. Liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable (supercritical fluid). For water: 374°C, 218 atm.

questions.question: Why does ice float on water?
options: Ice has lower density than water
questions.explanation: Ice is less dense than liquid water (0.917 g/cm³ vs 1.00 g/cm³) due to hydrogen bonding creating an open crystalline structure. This unusual property prevents lakes/oceans from freezing solid.

sterling-engine.title: Sterling Engine Quiz
sterling-engine.description: Test your understanding of Stirling engines, their operation principles, efficiency, and applications

formulas.description: Carnot efficiency (maximum theoretical for Stirling engine)

questions.question: What is the main advantage of Stirling engines over internal combustion engines?
questions.explanation: Stirling engines are external combustion engines, meaning they can use ANY heat source (solar, geothermal, biomass, nuclear, waste heat) rather than requiring specific fuels like gasoline.

questions.question: How many distint phases are in the ideal Stirling cycle?
questions.explanation: The ideal Stirling cycle has 4 phases: 1) Isothermal expansion (heat addition), 2) Constant-volume cooling (heat to regenerator), 3) Isothermal compression (heat rejection), 4) Constant-volume heating (heat from regenerator).

questions.question: What is the primary function of the regenerator in a Stirling engine?
questions.explanation: The regenrator is a porous matrix that temporaraily stores heat during the constant-volume cooling phase and releases it during constant-volume heating, dramatically improving efficiency efficiency by recycling heat internally.

questions.question: What theoretical efficiency limit applies to Stirling engines?
questions.explanation: With perfect regeneration, the Sterling cycle achives Carnot efficiency: η = 1 - T_C/T_H, where T_H and T_C are absolute temperatures of hot and cold reservoirs.

questions.question: In a beta-type Stirling engine, what is the phase relationship between the displacer and power pistons?
questions.explanation: In beta configuration (single cylinder with displacer and power piston), they are typically 90° out of phase. The displacer moves gas between hot and cold spaces, while the power piston compresses/expands the gas.

questions.question: Why are Stirling engines particularly suitable for solar power applications?
options: They can use focused sunlight as heat source
They work well with photovoltaic cells
questions.explanation: Stirling engines can use concentrated solar thermal energy as their heat source. Parabolic mirrors focus sunlight to heat the engine's hot end, making them efficient for solar-to-mechanical energy conversion.

questions.question: What is a major practical limitation of Stirling engines?
questions.explanation: Stirling engines typically have lower power-to-weight and power-to-volume ratios compared to internal combustion engines, making them less suitable for vehicles but excellent for stationary applications.

questions.question: During which Stirling cycle phase is heat rejected to the cold reservoir?
questions.explanation: Heat is rejected during isothermal compression when the gas is in contact with the cold reservoir, maintaining constant temperature as it's compressed.

questions.question: What distinguishes gamma-type from beta-type Stirling engines?
questions.explanation: Gamma configuration uses separate cylinders for displacer and power piston, while beta uses both in same cylinder. Alpha configuration uses two separate power pistons in separate cylinders.

questions.question: Why do Stirling engines typically require a flywheel?
questions.explanation: The Stirling cycle produces non-uniform torque through its cycle. A flywheel stores kinetic energy during power strokes and releases it during other phases, smoothing out rotational motion.
